hints: Think about which electron rich species attacks the strongly positive $\text{NO}_2^+$ in the first step, and where a curly arrow showing that attack must start.
Recall what happens to the aromatic ring when it forms a new bond to the electrophile, and how the positive charge is shown in the intermediate.
Consider how aromaticity is restored in the second step, and which bond must break to release a proton.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrophile and the nucleophile**
You have benzene meeting $\text{NO}_2^+$. The $\text{NO}_2^+$ is very electron poor because of the full positive charge on nitrogen, so it is the electrophile. Benzene is electron rich because of its delocalised $\pi$ system, so it acts as the nucleophile. Your first arrow must therefore start inside the benzene ring and point to the N atom.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
When that new $\text{C-N}$ bond forms, one carbon becomes tetrahedral and the delocalised ring is broken. Draw a cyclohexadienyl cation with $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{H}$ on the same $sp^3$ carbon, and a positive charge delocalised over the remaining five carbons, often shown with a horseshoe. This loss of aromaticity makes the intermediate high in energy.

Restore aromaticity by losing a proton**
Aromaticity is very stable, so there is a strong drive to get it back. The $\text{C-H}$ bond on the tetrahedral carbon breaks, and both electrons go back into the ring to reform the $\pi$ system. Show this with a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond into the ring, and show $\text{H}^+$ leaving to give nitrobenzene.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to N of $\text{NO}_2^+$ to give arenium intermediate with $\text{NO}_2$ bonded to ring, positive charge delocalised in ring and $\text{H}$ on same carbon.
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to restore aromaticity, with loss of $\text{H}^+$ to give nitrobenzene.

hints: Remember $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as a catalyst, so the $\text{HSO}_4^-$ formed when $\text{NO}_2^+$ is generated must pick up the $\text{H}^+$ lost in (a)(i).
walkthrough:
See why regeneration must happen**
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is called a catalyst in Table 6.1, so it cannot be used up. In making $\text{NO}_2^+$, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ donates a proton and becomes $\text{HSO}_4^-$. In the mechanism you just drew, a proton $\text{H}^+$ is expelled when aromaticity returns. That base $\text{HSO}_4^-$ simply accepts that proton: $$\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$

hints: Recall the directing rules: an electron withdrawing $\text{COOH}$ group directs differently from an electron donating $\text{OH}$ group.
Think about which positions are activated for phenol and which are deactivated for benzoic acid, to select the major mono substituted isomer in each case.
walkthrough:
Apply the director for benzoic acid**
The $\text{-COOH}$ group withdraws electron density from the ring and deactivates ortho and para positions most strongly. Electrophilic attack therefore occurs mainly at the meta position, which is least deactivated. So draw benzoic acid with $\text{NO}_2$ meta to $\text{COOH}$ to give 3-nitrobenzoic acid.

Apply the director for phenol**
The $\text{-OH}$ group donates electron density into the ring and strongly activates ortho and para positions. The electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$ therefore attacks ortho or para to $\text{OH}$. Draw 2-nitrophenol or 4-nitrophenol as the major mononitration product.

Final answer: From benzoic acid: 3-nitrobenzoic acid, $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ in 1,3 meta positions.
From phenol: 2-nitrophenol ($\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ ortho) or 4-nitrophenol ($\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ para).

hints: Use Table 6.1 to rank ease: which compound nitrates with dilute acid at $20^\circ\text{C}$ and which needs concentrated acid at $100^\circ\text{C}$.
Focus on the oxygen atom in phenol and what its lone pair can do with the benzene $\pi$ system.
Focus on the $\text{COOH}$ group in benzoic acid and whether it pushes electrons toward or pulls electrons away from the ring.
Link change in ring electron density to attraction for the positive $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile.
walkthrough:
Read the conditions as evidence**
Do not guess the order, read it from Table 6.1. Phenol nitrates with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at only $20^\circ\text{C}$, benzene needs concentrated acids at $50^\circ\text{C}$, benzoic acid needs concentrated acids at $100^\circ\text{C}$. Milder conditions means easier reaction, so the order is phenol easiest, then benzene, then benzoic acid hardest.

Explain phenol activation**
Look at the $\text{-OH}$ group. Oxygen has a lone pair in a p-orbital that can overlap with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the ring. This delocalisation pushes extra electron density into the ring. A more electron rich ring attracts the positive $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile more strongly, so the first step of electrophilic substitution is faster.

Explain benzoic acid deactivation**
Now look at $\text{-COOH}$. The $\text{C=O}$ part is strongly electron withdrawing. It pulls electron density out of the ring toward itself. This lowers the electron density in the ring compared with benzene, so the ring is less able to donate to $\text{NO}_2^+$ and attack is slower.

Tie structure to reactivity**
Put it together as cause and effect. Higher ring electron density means stronger attraction for an electrophile and easier nitration. Lower ring electron density means weaker attraction and harder nitration. That is why phenol is activated relative to benzene, while benzoic acid is deactivated relative to benzene.

Final answer: phenol > benzene > benzoic acid, easiest to least easy.
Phenol: lone pair in p-orbital on O delocalises / overlaps into ring $\pi$ system, increasing electron density in ring, ring attracts / polarises $\text{NO}_2^+$ more strongly.
Benzoic acid: $\text{COOH}$ is electron withdrawing, decreasing electron density in ring, ring attracts $\text{NO}_2^+$ less strongly.

hints: Work backwards from Congo Red: the central biphenyl unit comes from X and Z, so compare its substituents with the starting dinitro compound.
Use the molecular formula $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{12}\text{N}_2$ for X to decide what the two $\text{NO}_2$ groups have become in step 1.

Use the formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_8\text{NO}_3\text{SNa}$ for Y and the two naphthalene ends of Congo Red to deduce the coupling component, remembering Z must contain two diazonium groups for double coupling.
walkthrough:
Deduce X by comparing start and product**
The starting material is 4,4'-dinitrobiphenyl, $\text{O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NO}_2$. In Congo Red the central unit is the same biphenyl skeleton but linked through $\text{-N=N-}$ groups to naphthalenes. That means the $\text{NO}_2$ groups must first have become $\text{NH}_2$ groups. Check the formula: $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{12}\text{N}_2$ fits $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH}_2$, 4,4'-diaminobiphenyl.

Deduce Z as the double diazonium salt**
Step 2 must convert amines into diazonium ions for azo coupling in step 3. Since X is a diamine and Congo Red has two azo links from the central biphenyl outward, Z must be the bis-diazonium species: $^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+$, with both $\text{-N}_2^+$ groups para to the central bond.

Deduce Y as the naphthalene coupling partner**
Each end of Congo Red is a naphthalene bearing one $\text{NH}_2$, one $\text{SO}_3^-\text{Na}^+$ and one azo link ortho to $\text{NH}_2$. The formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_8\text{NO}_3\text{SNa}$ matches a sodium aminonaphthalene sulfonate. So Y is that substituted naphthalene, with $\text{-SO}_3^-\text{Na}^+$ unchanged, which couples to Z in alkaline $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to give the two $\text{-N=N-}$ bridges.

Final answer: X: $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH}_2$, 4,4'-diaminobiphenyl with $\text{NH}_2$ groups para to central bond.
Z: $^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+$, bis-diazonium ion with $\text{-N}_2^+$ groups para to central bond, 4,4'-biphenyl bis(diazonium).
Y: sodium 4-aminonaphthalene-1-sulfonate, naphthalene with $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{SO}_3^-\text{Na}^+$ groups positioned to allow coupling ortho to $\text{NH}_2$ as in Congo Red.

hints: Recall the standard way to convert $\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_2$ using a metal and acid with heating.
Remember that the reduction mixture is acidic and needs neutralisation to liberate the free amine.
Recall the reagents that generate nitrous acid in situ for conversion of $\text{-NH}_2$ to $\text{-N}_2^+$ and the critical low temperature required.
walkthrough:
Choose reduction conditions for step 1**
Step 1 is $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$. The classic A Level method is tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid: $$\text{Ar-NO}_2 + 6[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{Ar-NH}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ using $\text{Sn}$ / conc. $\text{HCl}$ with heating under reflux. Excess $\text{NaOH}$ is then added to neutralise the acid and release the free diamine X.

Choose diazotisation conditions for step 2**
Step 2 is $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ to $\text{Ar-N}_2^+$. This needs nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, made in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid: $$\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{HNO}_2 + \text{NaCl}$$

Control the temperature**
Diazonium salts decompose readily above about $10^\circ\text{C}$, releasing nitrogen gas. So the mixture must be kept cold, typically $0$ to $10^\circ\text{C}$ in an ice bath, to keep Z stable for coupling in step 3.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{Sn}$ and concentrated $\text{HCl}$, heat / reflux, followed by $\text{NaOH}$ to liberate amine.
step 2: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (to make $\text{HNO}_2$) with temperature $\leqslant 10^\circ\text{C}$.
